key_facts: **Lyme disease** is infection with *Borrelia burgdorferi* sensu lato from an infected **Ixodes tick** bite.
**Erythema migrans**: an expanding red patch (often over 5 cm) appearing 1–4 weeks after the bite: diagnose clinically, no tests needed (NICE NG95).
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily or 200 mg once daily for 21 days; amoxicillin or azithromycin as alternatives.
Remove ticks with fine-tipped tweezers or a tick tool; no prophylaxis or serology after an asymptomatic bite.
Later disease: facial palsy, meningitis, carditis, arthritis, acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans: specialist.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Lyme disease is a tick-borne infection with *Borrelia burgdorferi* sensu lato. It is the commonest tick-borne infection in the UK, and **the skin is the commonest presenting organ**.

**Erythema migrans (EM)** is the hallmark of early localised disease. **Acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans (ACA)** is a late cutaneous sign (months to years later), seen almost only in European Lyme (*B. afzelii*). Borrelial lymphocytoma (bluish nodule on earlobe, nipple or scrotum) is a less common early European feature.

sub: UK: a few thousand cases a year; New Forest, Exmoor, South Downs, Lake District, Scottish Highlands.
Peak May–September; walkers, gardeners, outdoor workers.

ul: Vector: hard tick ***Ixodes ricinus*** (sheep/deer tick). Tiny nymphs cause most infections. **Most bites do not transmit**; risk rises after about 24–48 hours of attachment, so prompt correct removal helps (NICE NG95).
UK risk: grassy/wooded areas, parks and gardens — higher in southern England and the Scottish Highlands, but possible anywhere. Peak spring–autumn.
EM: dermal spread from the bite. Dissemination can cause multiple EM, neuroborreliosis, carditis and arthritis.
ACA: chronic skin infection on acral extensors, often without a remembered bite.
Ixodes ricinus ticks; transmission usually needs prolonged attachment (over 24 hours).
**"No bull's-eye, no Lyme"**: most EM is uniformly red, not target-like.
**"A negative blood test excludes it"**: serology is often negative in early EM.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Borrelia spreads **outwards in the skin** from the bite, then through the blood.

mech.t: An infected tick feeds for over a day; spirochaetes migrate from tick gut to saliva.
Borrelia spreads centrifugally in the dermis, causing the expanding erythema migrans.
mech.caption: Erythema migrans expanding outwards from the bite site.

mech.t: Spirochaetes spread to the nervous system, heart, joints and other skin sites.
Persistent infection causes arthritis or acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans.
Prompt correct tick removal reduces transmission.
mech.caption: Grasp close to the skin and pull steadily up.

histo: Not needed for EM. Serology (ELISA then immunoblot) for suspected disseminated disease.

ul: A **red rash that enlarges** over days; may have central clearing (“bull’s-eye”), but many lesions are uniformly red or bluish.
Usually **not** hot, itchy or painful. Appears **3 days to 3 months** after a bite (commonly 1–4 weeks).
Often ≥5 cm at the bite site (legs, groin, axillae, beltline; head/neck in children). Harder to see in darker skin (bruise-like).
May accompany flu-like non-focal symptoms.

blocks.title: Not EM
blocks.text: A tick-bite reaction that appears and fades within about 48 hours, and is hot, itchy or painful, is local hypersensitivity — not Lyme.

ul: **Inflammatory stage:** bluish-red doughy discolouration of an extensor limb (hand, forearm, lower leg), often unilateral.
**Atrophic stage:** thin “cigarette-paper” skin with visible veins — easily mistaken for ageing or venous disease.
Often accompanies sensory neuropathy; mostly older women with European exposure.

variants.name: ACA atrophic
variants.t: Cigarette-paper skin, visible veins. *Site: Extensor limbs.*

sub: Amoxicillin in pregnancy; children under 12 per NG95 weight-based doses or specialist advice.

ul: **EM: diagnose and treat clinically. No blood test** — early serology is often negative (NG95).
Without EM (including suspected ACA): clinical picture plus **ELISA then immunoblot** via a UKAS-accredited lab. ACA is nearly always strongly IgG-positive.
**Do not** diagnose or test after an asymptomatic tick bite.
Do not rely on private “Lyme specialty” panels without checking accreditation.
Absence of a remembered bite does **not** exclude Lyme.

ddx.name: Tick-bite hypersensitivity
ddx.f: Within hours, fades ≤ 48 h, itchy / hot, small.

ddx.name: Tinea corporis
ddx.f: Scaly active edge; EM is not scaly.

ddx.name: Granuloma annulare
ddx.f: Chronic firm papular ring; no daily expansion.

ddx.name: ACA mimics
ddx.f: Chilblains, venous disease, morphoea, ageing skin.

ul: Cover skin, use DEET-type repellent, and check skin folds/scalp after outdoor activity.
Remove ticks with **fine-tipped tweezers or a tick tool**: grasp close to the skin and pull steadily up — do not twist, crush, burn or smother with oils (UKHSA).
**No antibiotic prophylaxis or serology** after an asymptomatic bite. Watch the site for weeks and return if a spreading rash or flu-like illness appears.

blocks.h: Erythema migrans (adults / ≥12 years, no focal symptoms) — NICE NG95

head: Choice
Regimen
Duration
rows: Doxycycline 100 mg BD or 200 mg OD
Azithromycin 500 mg OD (avoid in carditis / QT risk)

ul: Doxycycline: take upright with water; separate from antacids/iron/calcium; sun protection; avoid in pregnancy and under 12.
Pregnancy: usually **amoxicillin** after assessment.
Children under 12 / under 18 with more than a single uncomplicated EM: discuss with a specialist (NG95).
Warn about a self-limiting **Jarisch–Herxheimer** flu-like flare in the first day or two — keep taking the antibiotic.
Refer for confirmation (serology ± biopsy).
Adult ACA: doxycycline (or amoxicillin) for **28 days** per NG95; IV ceftriaxone is a second alternative.
Atrophy and neuropathy may not reverse — set expectations.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Two courses done, still symptomatic**: No more antibiotics: specialist / reference-lab advice.

refer.t: Meningitis / encephalitis signs, carditis or heart block, uveitis.
Facial palsy, radiculopathy, inflammatory arthritis, multiple EM with systemic upset: discuss with specialist **without delaying antibiotics**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Emergency pathways even if Lyme is possible: meningitis/encephalitis signs, uveitis, carditis or complete heart block.
Same-day/urgent GP: facial palsy, radiculopathy, inflammatory arthritis, multiple EM with systemic upset — discuss with a specialist without delaying antibiotics.
Persistent symptoms after two completed antibiotic courses: do not give more antibiotics; seek specialist/reference-lab advice.
Neuroborreliosis, carditis (heart block), arthritis, ACA.
Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction on starting treatment.
EM treated promptly has an excellent outlook; some have lingering fatigue.

pearls: **Expanding red ring after the outdoors = treat. Don’t test.**
Draw round the edge and photograph to monitor spread.
A full **21-day** course matters for EM.
Reinfection is possible — infection does not confer lasting immunity.
ACA is often missed as “poor circulation” in an older person’s limb — ask about European countryside exposure and test.
